brief: Bloomberg macro strategist Simon White argues persistently squeezed liquidity, not day-to-day headlines like a Taiwan labor strike threat or soaring sovereign yields, is the real drag on stocks. Excess liquidity (real M1 growth minus economic growth) turned negative in early June. It acts on risk assets with a three-to-six month lag, so the market is now in the window where the drag should show up. Rising inflation has diverted money that would otherwise support growth toward higher nominal growth instead. Financial conditions have also tightened globally: the annual change in the median real 10-year rate is positive and rising for the first time since late 2022. US real rates rose for most of the year as markets gave new Fed chair Kevin Warsh a hawkish pass. Doubt crept in through August and yields retraced somewhat, but Warsh's Jackson Hole speech confirmed he will not let inflation run out of control. Falling liquidity combined with its rising price explains why stocks are chopping sideways and are more exposed to negative headlines. White expects a corrective selloff of roughly 10-15%, but says a deeper drop is unlikely while recession risk stays low.
